coherence.reasons: Both run a clean diagnosis-to-plan-to-first-moves hierarchy with sized sections that roll up to the total. X's pyramid is very orderly, but its governing thought has two tensions. It says "not wages" while targeted labor ($7.3M) is its single largest lever and sits in the first wave. It also headlines 3.2%, a figure that excludes the known 2027 wage rise; X's own backup shows 2.7% with the rise unanswered. Y's governing thought (~2.9–3.1%, rebalance labor, no 8% cut) matches what its bridge, options table and scenarios actually show, and its board decisions follow directly from the storyline.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred answer: reprice delivery, prune losing promotions, fix shrink, grow private label, exit weak stores, and replace the blanket cut with a targeted one. Y weighs alternatives better. It scores five options on operating income, margin, one-time cost and constraint fit, including the management draft ($13–26M, 0.9–1.7%) and exiting home delivery (~3.3% but breaks the owners' commitment). It puts the wage step in the base case, admits the base lands at 2.9%, and names the stretch that closes the gap. It adds a low/base/high range, stage gates, reversal triggers and a contingency it says covers one failure but not two. It also budgets one-time costs ($20.1M, flagged as allowances) and nets a 1% volume loss against the promotion cut. X weighs 8% versus 4% labor and six versus nine stores well, and has good tracking measures. But its labor lever is aggressive: a net 4% of chain hours taken only from Q3–Q4 stores is a much deeper cut in those stores, resting on the assumption that shrink stays flat. Its promotion reset assumes no volume loss, it budgets no one-time cost beyond the $7.5M lease exit, and it leans on demanding stretch levers to absorb the wage rise.

evidence.reasons: Both are numerically accurate on the critical items: the margin bridge, the labor wage/hours split, the −$10.4M e-commerce result, −$12.34 per delivered order, the fee-test rollout (~$2.5–2.8M) and store exits at $6.6M. Both rebuild the fulfillment line and dismantle the 6.1% claim. Y adds a dollar bridge reconciled to the $32.6M fall, a break-even test of the category team's comp claim, a click-and-collect break-even, and a consistent post-exit sales base. Y's weak spots are the vendor-funding sizing, which rests on a speculative reading of the 14-point gap (flagged, and zeroed in the low case), and the assumption that half the wage step is recovered in prices. X is more restrained in declining to size vendor funding, and it carefully nets $1.3M of overlap out of store exits. But X infers that promotions "have not held off ValuMart" without a counterfactual, sizes its largest lever (net 4% labor) as a "team choice" with thin support, and leaves the wage rise out of its base case. On balance Y uses the evidence slightly more rigorously.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage hypothesis: labor is about 13% of the decline, fewer hours absorbed about 70% of the wage effect, and the blanket cut is replaced with a targeted one because of the shrink link. Both also replace the e-commerce freeze with repricing. Y goes further in two ways. It quantifies where the management plan would land (0.9–1.7%, short of target even at best), and it tests its own counter-hypothesis that commercial fixes alone suffice, finds it reaches only ~2.1%, and updates to add labor rebalancing and store exits. It keeps the defensible part of the freeze (no growth until orders make money) with a stated rationale. X's revision is sound and well evidenced but less explicit about what was tested and what was kept.

overall.reasons: Both documents meet the key's defensibility criteria: a quantified bridge, sized levers that roughly reach 3.0%, and second-order effects acknowledged. Y would serve the CEO better at the board. Its headline includes the wage step and admits a 2.9% base. It compares options quantitatively, budgets the $25M cap, gives a downside range, and sets gates, triggers and contingencies. It ends with explicit board decisions, including a covenant fallback (waiver discussion) and confirming the delivery commitment with the owners. X is rigorous and well structured, but its 3.2% headline depends on excluding a known wage rise, its largest lever is a thinly supported labor cut, and it does not budget implementation costs.
